subject: Baughan et al. (1968)
object: Baughan et al. (1968) reported hereditary hemolytic anemia associated with glucosephosphate isomerase (GPI) deficiency, describing it as a new enzyme defect of human erythrocytes.

subject: Detter et al. (1968)
object: Detter et al. (1968) studied inherited variations in human phosphohexose isomerase (glucose phosphate isomerase).

subject: Hutton (1969)
object: Hutton (1969) used biochemical variants in mice to show linkage between the hemoglobin beta-chain locus and the glucosephosphate isomerase locus.

subject: Paglia et al. (1969)
object: Paglia et al. (1969) reported that defective hexosephosphate isomerization occurred in both human erythrocytes and leukocytes.

subject: Blume and Beutler (1972)
object: Blume and Beutler (1972) described a screening procedure for detecting glucose-phosphate isomerase deficiency.

subject: Blume et al. (1972)
object: Blume et al. (1972) characterized two new variants of glucose-phosphate-isomerase deficiency associated with hereditary nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia.

subject: Nakashima et al. (1973)
object: Nakashima et al. (1973) carried out electrophoretic and kinetic studies of glucosephosphate isomerase (GPI) in two unrelated Japanese families with GPI deficiency.

subject: Hutton and Chilcote (1974)
object: Hutton and Chilcote (1974) described 8 children (5 living, 3 deceased) from 2 families in Kentucky and Indiana with severe hereditary nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia caused by glucose phosphate isomerase deficiency. All affected children were severely anemic in early life. Three deaths occurred in young patients who did not receive adequate blood transfusions or whose parents refused to permit splenectomy. Growth and development were surprisingly normal, and no patient died of infection.

subject: Hutton and Chilcote (1974)
object: Hutton and Chilcote (1974) found that in patients with glucose phosphate isomerase deficiency, splenectomy generally abolished the requirement for blood transfusion, and no patient required regular transfusion after puberty.

subject: Hutton and Chilcote (1974)
object: Hutton and Chilcote (1974) concluded that the anemia due to glucose phosphate isomerase deficiency was expressed as an autosomal recessive trait, although the enzyme variant could be detected in hematologically normal heterozygotes.

subject: Hutton and Chilcote (1974)
object: Hutton and Chilcote (1974) found that the abnormal glucose phosphate isomerase molecule was heat labile and was present in neutrophils and lymphocytes as well as in erythrocytes.

subject: Paglia and Valentine (1974)
object: Paglia and Valentine (1974) reviewed hereditary glucosephosphate isomerase deficiency.

subject: Beutler et al. (1974)
object: Beutler et al. (1974) reported glucosephosphate isomerase (GPI) deficiency due to a variant they named GPI Elyria.

subject: GPI GPI elyria
object: GPI

subject: Paglia et al. (1975)
object: Paglia et al. (1975) studied a Mexican kindred with a unique erythrocyte glucosephosphate isomerase phenotype, which they called GPI Valle Hermoso. The proband's isozyme showed decreased activity and marked thermal instability. Its kinetics, pH optimum and starch gel electrophoretic pattern were normal.

subject: GPI GPI Valle Hermoso
object: GPI

subject: Paglia et al. (1975)
object: Paglia et al. (1975) concluded that the proband was apparently homozygous for a mutant autosomal allele that governs production of the GPI Valle Hermoso isozyme.

subject: Paglia et al. (1975)
object: Unlike in previously known cases, leukocyte and plasma GPI activities were unimpaired in the proband. Paglia et al. (1975) suggested that the structural alteration mainly made the enzyme unstable without greatly reducing its catalytic effectiveness, so that cells able to keep synthesizing protein could compensate. However, density-gradient fractionation of the affected erythrocytes did not show age-related losses of GPI.

subject: Van Biervliet et al. (1975)
object: Van Biervliet et al. (1975) described a new variant of glucose-6-phosphate isomerase deficiency in a patient and studied the kinetics and properties of the enzyme. They compared their data with the other variants reported in the literature up to that time.

subject: Van Biervliet et al. (1975)
object: Van Biervliet et al. (1975) reported that genetic and electrophoretic data pointed to a double heterozygous state in their patient with glucosephosphate isomerase deficiency.

subject: Van Biervliet et al. (1975)
object: Van Biervliet et al. (1975) described a new case of glucosephosphate isomerase deficiency in a Dutch family, with enzyme activity reduced to 20-25% of normal. The mutant enzyme was markedly thermolabile, losing 90% of its activity after 1 hour at 45 degrees C. Its pH optimum and electrophoretic migration were normal, and its Km for F-6-P and its Ki values for the competitive inhibitors 2,3-DPG and 6-PG were within the normal range. Because this variant differed from all known variants, the authors proposed naming it GPI-Utrecht.

subject: GPI GPI-Utrecht
object: GPI

subject: Rotteveel et al. (1977)
object: Rotteveel et al. (1977) reported a patient from a Dutch family with glucosephosphate isomerase deficiency, type Nijmegen. The patient had nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia that presented in the neonatal period. The degree of hemolysis stayed about the same over the years, but trivial infections often triggered increased hemolysis that required blood transfusions.

subject: Rotteveel et al. (1977)
object: Rotteveel et al. (1977) found on enzyme studies that the patient's GPI deficiency was caused by a double heterozygous state for two different GPI-deficient alleles. The parents and grandparents each carried one of these deficient alleles but showed no sign of hemolysis, such as shortened red-cell survival.

subject: Galand et al. (1978)
object: Galand et al. (1978) described a 6-year-old girl with glucosephosphate isomerase deficiency and mild hemolytic anemia.

subject: Galand et al. (1978)
object: Galand et al. (1978) found that the deficient GPI enzyme in their patient had profoundly decreased red cell activity, a normal electrophoretic phenotype, normal isoelectric point, normal optimum pH, molecular instability, and a clearly decreased Michaelis constant for fructose-6-phosphate.

subject: Galand et al. (1978)
object: Galand et al. (1978) concluded that their patient was a double (compound) heterozygote for a 'silent gene' inherited from the mother and an abnormal enzyme inherited from the father; because the paternal abnormal enzyme had undescribed characteristics, they proposed the name GPI-Mytho for this new variant.

subject: GPI GPI-MYTHO
object: GPI

subject: GPI 'silent gene'
object: GPI

subject: Kahn et al. (1978)
object: Kahn et al. (1978) described patients with severe chronic hemolytic anemia due to deficient glucose phosphate isomerase (GPI) variants. The patients' parents were consanguineous, and the patients were considered true homozygotes for the mutated GPI genes.

subject: Kahn et al. (1978)
object: Kahn et al. (1978) found that in both GPI variants the main cause of the enzyme deficiency was molecular instability of the mutant GPI, with nearly normal catalytic activity. GPI 'Paris' showed slow electrophoretic migration and drastically altered substrate affinity (decreased for glucose-6-phosphate, increased for fructose-6-phosphate).

subject: GPI GPI 'Paris'
object: GPI

subject: Kahn et al. (1978)
object: Kahn et al. (1978) characterized GPI 'Enfants malades', an unstable variant with slightly reduced electrophoretic mobility, an abnormal pH-activity curve, and an abnormal ratio of maximal velocity in the backward (fructose-6-phosphate to glucose-6-phosphate) versus forward direction.

subject: GPI GPI 'Enfants malades'
object: GPI

subject: Kahn et al. (1978)
object: Kahn et al. (1978) could not prove a clear relation between the kinetic abnormalities of the mutant GPI variants and the metabolic changes of GPI-deficient red cells or the severity of hemolysis.

subject: Kahn et al. (1978)
object: Kahn et al. (1978) emphasized a possible role of impairment of the hexose monophosphate pathway in the reduced viability of GPI-deficient red cells.

subject: Zanella et al. (1978)
object: Zanella et al. (1978) reported a patient with congenital nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia who had a new abnormal glucosephosphate isomerase (GPI), reduced glutathione (GSH) deficiency, GSH instability, and altered carbohydrate composition of the erythrocyte membrane.

subject: Zanella et al. (1978)
object: Zanella et al. (1978) found that the only functional abnormality of the patient's mutant GPI appeared to be marked instability to heat, urea, and guanidine-HCl. Incubating normal and patient GPI with oxidizing and reducing agents suggested that the abnormality was in the SH groups of the mutant enzyme.

subject: Zanella et al. (1978)
object: Family studies by Zanella et al. (1978) suggested that the propositus was doubly heterozygous. One allele, from the mother, was a gene producing an inactive enzyme. The other, from the father, was a gene with a structural alteration that made the encoded GPI markedly labile.

subject: Arnold (1979)
object: Arnold (1979) reviewed glucosephosphate isomerase (GPI) deficiency, first reported in 1967, and noted that patients from all over the world suffer from a typical nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia with hemolytic crises during acute infections.

subject: Arnold (1979)
object: Arnold (1979) stated that GPI deficiency is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, with half of the patients being homozygotes and the others compound (double) heterozygotes.

subject: Arnold (1979)
object: Arnold (1979) noted that the biochemical properties of the deficient GPI enzymes vary widely, so many well-characterized enzymes have been designated as different variants; alterations of physicochemical properties exceeded kinetic aberrations, and all defective variants were more or less unstable.

subject: Arnold (1979)
object: Arnold (1979) reported that GPI activity diminishes progressively in deficient red cells, leading to a rise in glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) concentration and, after in vitro aging, to dramatic impairment of glycolysis and concomitant hemolysis; the metabolic block was attributed to diminished GPI activity itself rather than inhibition of hexokinase by high G6P.

subject: Isacchi et al. (1979)
object: Isacchi et al. (1979) described a 5-year-old Italian girl, born to first-cousin parents, with severe congenital hemolytic anemia and proven red cell glucose phosphate isomerase (GPI) deficiency.

subject: Isacchi et al. (1979)
object: Isacchi et al. (1979) found that the new variant, GPI Roma, was slightly heat-unstable and had a slightly increased Michaelis constant for fructose-6-phosphate. The patient's white cells showed a single predominant fast-migrating GPI form, whereas red cells showed this fast band plus a major band migrating as normal GPI and an additional slow band; the authors showed this could be ascribed to postsynthetic events modifying the charge of the mutant enzyme.

subject: GPI GPI Roma
object: GPI

subject: Isacchi et al. (1979)
object: Isacchi et al. (1979) showed that both first-cousin parents of the affected girl were heterozygous for the GPI Roma variant, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

subject: Whitelaw et al. (1979)
object: Whitelaw et al. (1979) reported the first child of unrelated, healthy Caucasian parents, who had GPI deficiency with severe hemolysis and hydrops fetalis and died at 3 hours of age.

subject: Whitelaw et al. (1979)
object: Whitelaw et al. (1979) found that both parents of the affected child had 50% of normal red cell GPI activity, and qualitative studies of their red and white cells showed that each was heterozygous for a different GPI-deficiency variant allele; placental studies showed the propositus was a compound heterozygote.

subject: Whitelaw et al. (1979)
object: Whitelaw et al. (1979) found that the healthy heterozygous parents each had 50% of normal red cell GPI activity.

subject: Whitelaw et al. (1979)
object: Whitelaw et al. (1979) made a prenatal diagnosis of GPI deficiency by studying amniotic cells obtained by amniocentesis at 28 weeks in the mother's second pregnancy; the second child was a compound heterozygote at the GPI locus, indistinguishable from the first.

subject: Whitelaw et al. (1979)
object: Whitelaw et al. (1979) reported that the prenatally diagnosed second affected child was successfully treated with immediate exchange transfusion and later blood transfusions.

subject: Arnold et al. (1980)
object: Arnold et al. (1980) reported a 1-year-old German boy, born to consanguineous parents, with chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia and recurrent hemolytic crises caused by glucosephosphate isomerase (GPI) deficiency. Because of the parental consanguinity, the patient was considered a true homozygote.

subject: Arnold et al. (1980)
object: Arnold et al. (1980) found that the deficient GPI enzyme in their patient had altered electrophoretic mobility, pronounced thermolability, increased affinity for glucose-6-phosphate and for the competitive inhibitor 6-phosphogluconate, and slightly changed pH optima for both substrates. Electrophoresis after freezing and thawing of the hemolysate suggested that the subunit alteration affected conversion of the main band into secondary bands; the authors designated the new variant GPI Augsburg.

subject: GPI GPI Augsburg
object: GPI

subject: Zanella et al. (1980)
object: Zanella et al. (1980) described a new variant of glucosephosphate isomerase (GPI) associated with severe hemolytic anemia, mental retardation, and muscular hypotonia.

subject: Zanella et al. (1980)
object: Zanella et al. (1980) found that the defective GPI enzyme showed increased affinity for fructose-6-phosphate, decreased affinity for glucose-6-phosphate, altered electrophoretic and isoelectrofocusing patterns, and a left shift of the precipitin curve, but was stable to heat, urea, guanidine-HCl, and storage. Optimum pH, Ki for 6-phosphogluconic acid and erythrose-4-phosphate, molecular weight, GPI-related antigen concentration, immunodiffusion pattern, and immunoinactivation were normal. The authors stated this was the first example of a stable mutant GPI associated with severe hemolytic anemia, enzyme instability having been present in all previously reported cases.

subject: Arnold et al. (1981)
object: Arnold et al. (1981) described a 5-year-old boy of Italian origin who had a severe hemolytic crisis. His hemolysate showed hemizygous glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency together with heterozygous glucosephosphate isomerase (GPI) deficiency. The authors concluded that only the G6PD deficiency seemed to be responsible for the hemolytic crisis. They noted that this was the fourth family reported with combined deficiency of these two enzymes, whose genes lie on different chromosomes.

subject: Arnold et al. (1981)
object: Arnold et al. (1981) found heterozygous GPI deficiency and hemizygous G6PD deficiency in the red cells of an Italian boy. They reported that this was the fourth family in the literature with combined deficiency of these two enzymes.

subject: Arnold et al. (1983)
object: Arnold et al. (1983) described a 13-year-old German girl with chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia caused by GPI deficiency, with recurrent hemolytic crises that usually followed a febrile infection. She needed a blood transfusion during a crisis only once.

subject: Arnold et al. (1983)
object: Arnold et al. (1983) concluded from family studies that their patient with GPI deficiency was doubly heterozygous for the deficiency.

subject: Arnold et al. (1983)
object: Arnold et al. (1983) found that the deficient GPI enzyme in their patient showed altered electrophoretic migration, pronounced thermolability, increased affinity for glucose-6-phosphate, and slightly changed pH optima for both substrates. They designated it a new variant, GPI-Kaiserslautern.

subject: GPI GPI-Kaiserlautern
object: GPI

subject: Schröter et al. (1985)
object: Schröter et al. (1985) described a propositus with generalized glucosephosphate isomerase (GPI) deficiency who had a complex syndrome involving erythrocytes (congenital hemolytic anemia), granulocytes (decreased production of superoxide anion and reduced bactericidal activity in vitro), and the neuromuscular system (myopathy and mental retardation).

subject: Schröter et al. (1985)
object: Schröter et al. (1985) characterized a new GPI variant, GPI Homburg, with very low specific activity in erythrocytes, granulocytes, and muscle tissue, nearly normal stability, normal kinetic properties, and decreased electrophoretic mobility.

subject: GPI GPI Homburg
object: GPI

subject: Schröter et al. (1985)
object: Schröter et al. (1985) suggested that the clinical syndrome resulted from generalized GPI deficiency due to decreased specific activity of the variant enzyme, which could not be compensated by increased de novo synthesis of GPI protein even in cells with active protein synthesis such as granulocytes and muscle cells.

subject: Bonné-Tamir et al. (1987)
object: Bonné-Tamir et al. (1987) studied phosphoglucose isomerase (PGI) and 16 other biochemical genetic markers in an inbred Israeli-Arab family that had previously been described with hereditary adenylate kinase (AK) and G6PD deficiency. They found a rare PGI*3 allele in 11 of 32 family members tested. Its electrophoretic mobility was similar to the PGI*3 allele found in Indian populations, but unlike the Indian allele it had very low specific activity and heat stability.

subject: PGI PGI*3(Israel)
object: PGI

subject: Bonné-Tamir et al. (1987)
object: Bonné-Tamir et al. (1987) concluded that the distribution of the PGI*3(Israel) allele (11 of 32 members tested) in an inbred Israeli-Arab family indicated autosomal codominant inheritance.

subject: Bonné-Tamir et al. (1987)
object: Bonné-Tamir et al. (1987) designated the variant PGI*3(Israel) and suggested that it was a different, unstable mutation from the Indian PGI*3 allele. They also suggested that, together with the AK and G6PD deficiencies in the family, it seemed to be associated with severe anemia.

subject: Ravindranath et al. (1987)
object: Ravindranath et al. (1987) reported glucose phosphate isomerase deficiency as a cause of hydrops fetalis.

subject: Shalev et al. (1993)
object: Shalev et al. (1993) reported GPI deficiency in a 23-year-old Ashkenazi Jewish man who showed the typical clinical course of the disorder: chronic hemolysis, which improved after splenectomy. The authors stated this was the first report of GPI deficiency in a patient of Jewish descent.

subject: Shalev et al. (1993)
object: Shalev et al. (1993) found that the patient's GPI variant moved slowly on electrophoresis, showed only one of the two bands normally present, and was extremely thermolabile. They proposed naming it 'GPI Mount Scopus'.

subject: GPI GPI Mount Scopus
object: GPI

subject: Merkle and Pretsch (1993)
object: Merkle and Pretsch (1993) described the first 2 mutations causing hereditary GPI deficiency with chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia in a nonhuman mammal, the mouse. As in humans, the hemolytic syndrome (diminished erythrocyte number, lower hematocrit and hemoglobin, reticulocytosis, increased plasma bilirubin, and increased liver- and spleen-somatic indices) was manifested only in homozygous mutants; heterozygotes showed no hematologic or physiologic differences from wildtype.

subject: Merkle and Pretsch (1993)
object: Merkle and Pretsch (1993) found that, allowing for the young erythrocyte population, homozygous mutant mouse erythrocytes had increased glucose-6-phosphate, normal or decreased glycolytic metabolites distal to the block, and apparently reduced ATP and glycolytic rate. Homozygous anemic mice showed hepatosplenomegaly, adaptations to hypoxia (elevated heart-somatic index and, in one line, lung-somatic index), and marked reduction of body weight and increased lethality correlated with the degree of tissue enzyme deficiency, which the authors attributed to reduced glycolytic capability of the whole organism.

subject: Merkle and Pretsch (1993)
object: Merkle and Pretsch (1993) concluded that the similarity of physicochemical and kinetic properties of the mutant murine GPI proteins to human GPI-deficiency allozymes, and comparable metabolic and physiologic consequences, supported these mouse mutants as excellent models for human GPI deficiency.

subject: Walker et al. (1993)
object: Walker et al. (1993) reported DNA sequence abnormalities in patients with human glucose 6-phosphate isomerase deficiency.

subject: Kugler et al. (1998)
object: Kugler et al. (1998) studied 2 families with severe GPI deficiency. One patient (GPI Homburg) had nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia with additional neurological deficits, whereas 2 affected sibs in the second family (GPI Calden) showed no neurological symptoms.

subject: Kugler et al. (1998)
object: In the neurologically affected patient with GPI deficiency (GPI Homburg), Kugler et al. (1998) identified compound heterozygosity for a 59A-C transversion resulting in a his20-to-pro (H20P) substitution and a 1016T-C transition resulting in a leu339-to-pro (L339P) substitution in the GPI gene. The authors suggested that insertion of proline was likely to affect folding and activity of the enzyme.

subject: Kugler et al. (1998)
object: In 2 sibs with severe GPI deficiency without neurological symptoms (GPI Calden), Kugler et al. (1998) identified 1166A-G (H389R) and 1549C-G (L517V) mutations in the GPI gene, located at the subunit interface.

subject: Kugler et al. (1998)
object: Kugler et al. (1998) proposed that GPI mutations causing incorrect folding destroy both catalytic (GPI) and neurotrophic (neuroleukin) activities, leading to neurological symptoms (GPI Homburg), whereas alterations that allow correct folding retain neurotrophic properties (GPI Calden).
